hints: Remember what Km actually measures on a rate graph. It is the substrate concentration needed to get to exactly half of Vmax.
Ask yourself: if you only need a tiny bit of substrate to get to half speed, does that mean the enzyme grabs substrate easily or poorly?
walkthrough:
**Recall what Km really means**

Think of Km as a helpful number on the x-axis. It is the substrate concentration that gives you half of Vmax.

Key definition:
$$K_m = \text{substrate concentration when rate} = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$$

**Link low Km to high affinity**

If Km is low, you reach half speed with only a little substrate. That tells you the enzyme binds substrate very easily, even when there is not much around.

That is exactly what we mean by high affinity: strong attraction and quick formation of enzyme-substrate complexes.

**Check the opposite for high Km**

If Km is high, you need a lot of substrate to reach half speed. The enzyme is not good at grabbing substrate, so affinity is low and Vmax is only reached at high substrate concentration.

options.A: High Km means you need a lot of substrate to get going, so Vmax is reached at high, not low, substrate concentration.
options.B: This is back to front. High Km means low affinity, because much more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax.
options.C: Low Km means the enzyme works well at low substrate, so it reaches Vmax at a low, not high, substrate concentration.
options.D: Correct. Low Km means half Vmax is achieved with little substrate, which shows the enzyme has a high affinity for its substrate.
